title: Infra Team Wiki: GPU Fleet Capacity, CI/CD, and IaC (Ops)
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary

This ops-focused page consolidates the infra team’s operational guidance for GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD build pipelines, and runbooks. It is intended for oncall engineers, SREs, and infra module owners. The page contains ownership, SLOs, capacity planning cadence, Terraform best-practices, CI gates, and concise runbooks for common incidents.

Owners and contacts

- Primary owner: infra-capacity@redwood.com (team: infra-engineering)
- Runbook & oncall lead: Miguel Torres
- IaC & Terraform lead: Emily Chen
- Networking & cloud accounts: Ravi Kumar
- Slack channels: #infra-gpu, #infra-ops, #infra-iac, #pagerduty-infra

High-level goals

- Maintain GPU node pool availability >= 99.5% per-region per-month.
- Keep median node utilization between 55-75% to balance cost vs headroom.
- Ensure CI pipelines validate all IaC changes with policy and integration tests prior to prod apply.
- Maintain concise runbooks for top incidents: OOMs, driver failures, node terminations, IP exhaustion, autoscaler regressions, Terraform drift.

GPU fleet & capacity planning

Overview

GPU fleet supports model serving (hosted, dedicated) and internal eval/train workloads. Fleets are organized by region and class: small inference (A100 40GB), large inference (H100 80GB), spot pools, and reserved pools. Planning is monthly with weekly health checks.

Key SLOs and targets

- Node availability SLO: 99.5% (region/month)
- Fleet scale-up latency: P95 < 6 minutes (from autoscaler decision to node Ready)
- Median GPU utilization target: 55-75% (sustained >72h at >72% triggers CR)
- Spot preemption tolerance: < 2% request failure rate due to lack of fallback capacity

Capacity headroom policy

- Maintain at least 20% headroom (reserved-capacity-equivalent) for production customers per-region.
- If utilization >75% for 72h, open a Capacity Request (CR) in JIRA and escalate if forecasted shortfall >10% in next 7 days.

Forecasting and cadences

1. Monthly capacity review: infra + demand owners review usage and commit to reserved purchases or on-demand spend.
2. Weekly health check: automated dashboard with 24h/72h trends; alerts on threshold crossings.
3. Quarterly reserved commit planning: recommend reserved purchases where 6-month forecast favors commitment.

Required dashboards and metrics

- Per-region GPU counts (ready vs not-ready)
- Per-GPU-type utilization metrics: vram_used, gpu_util, pod_count
- Preemption and spot fallback events
- Autoscaler metrics: scale_up_count, scale_down_count, failed_scale_ops
- Alerts: node-unready >5 nodes for 10m, region-utilization >85% for 1h

Capacity request process (CR)

1. Create CR in JIRA (project INFRA-CR) with forecast window, requested GPUs, regions, and cost estimate.
2. Attach dashboard screenshots and forecast spreadsheet (infra/capacity/forecasts).
3. Owner review within 24h; procurement & finance review within 72h for reserved purchases.
4. Provision via infra runbooks and IaC (see Runbooks section).

Cloud accounts and networking

Account structure

- Root organization: redwood-cloud-org
- Accounts: infra-prod-<region>, infra-staging, infra-dev, demo, security-logging
- Tagging policy: project, owner, environment, cost-center; tag enforcement via pre-commit and CI.

Networking patterns

- VPC per account; shared-services VPC for monitoring and ingestion; VPC peering or transit gateway for control plane traffic.
- Standard subnets: public (nat-gw), private (workers), db (restricted). GPU nodes in private subnets only.
- Egress via centralized NAT gateway cluster to provide stable egress IPs for whitelisting.

Connectivity & security

- Transit gateway/cloud-router for cross-account traffic.
- IP planning: allocate /20 per region for worker pools; track allocations in infra/ip-alloc spreadsheet.
- Security groups: restrict inbound, allow kubelet health probes and registry egress.

Networking run issues and mitigations

- IP exhaustion: short-term reassign worker pools to alternate subnets; long-term expand VPC CIDR or reorganize allocations.
- NAT saturation: scale NAT targets and route heavy egress through managed transfer services.

Terraform/IaC modules and best practices

Module registry (recommended)

- redwood/vpc: VPC, subnets, routes, NAT config
- redwood/gpu-node-pool: ASG/instance group, driver bootstrap, kubelet config
- redwood/iam: roles, service-accounts, least-privilege policies
- redwood/eks-cluster: cluster bootstrap, managed nodegroups, addons
- redwood/monitoring: cloud exporters, datadog/prometheus configs

Module guidance

- Publish modules to internal Terraform Registry with semantic versioning.
- Changes to public infra (VPC, IAM) require security review and a two-week change advisory window for prod-impacting changes.
- Avoid hard-coded account IDs; use variables and lookups.

Example module usage (snippet)

```
module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repo.internal/redwood/terraform-modules.git//gpu-node-pool?ref=v1.7.0"
  name   = "prod-gpu-h100-1"
  region = "us-west-2"
  instance_type = "hpc-gpu-h100"
  desired_count  = 12
  min_count = 4
  max_count = 40
}
```

IaC review & merge policy

- IaC PRs must include: terraform plan output, cost delta estimate, and security scan results.
- Require 2 approvals for prod module changes; one approver must be security or infra-sre.
- Enforce terraform plan + policy checks (OPA) in CI before apply.

CI/CD and build pipelines

Pipeline overview

- Repo layout: infra-modules/*, infra-live/* (per-account roots), cluster-configs/*
- CI runner: self-hosted runners in infra-ci account with scoped permissions; PRs run plan-only, gated merges run plan+apply in staging.
- Deploy flow: PR -> CI plan -> staging apply (automated) -> manual approval -> prod apply.

Gates and automated checks

- Static checks: terraform fmt, tflint, terragrunt (where applicable)
- Security: policy-as-code (OPA), IAM diff detection, secret scanning
- Integration tests: apply to ephemeral env or staging; smoke tests: kube node readiness and sample GPU pod scheduling

Artifacts and provenance

- Module artifacts stored in internal registry with checksums.
- Retain plan artifacts for 90 days linked to PR.
- CI build logs retained for 30 days (extendable for investigations).

CI failure modes and troubleshooting

1. Provider auth failures: verify runner role or service principal expiry and refresh credentials.
2. Drift detected in plan: reconcile by applying changes to staging and investigate manual console edits.
3. Long apply times: split changes into smaller steps; avoid broad subnet changes.

Runbooks (operational playbooks)

Top-level runbooks (quick links)

- GPU node OOM / MIG OOM troubleshooting
- Node driver or CUDA failure (driver reload procedures)
- Autoscaler stuck / failing to scale
- IP exhaustion mitigation
- Terraform drift & emergency rollback
- Reserved capacity provisioning playbook

Example: GPU node OOM runbook (abridged)

1. Trigger: pod OOM count >5 in 10m or GPU memory usage >95% for 5m across pods.
2. PagerDuty: oncall starts the runbook.
3. Mitigation: cordon affected node(s): `kubectl cordon <node>`; evict heavy pods: `kubectl delete pod <pod> --namespace`.
4. If repeat: scale up nodepool +20% via Terraform var patch or trigger autoscaler override.
5. Post-incident: collect nvpeer-smi dump, kube events, node-exporter metrics; attach to incident ticket.

Autoscaler failure runbook (abridged)

- Symptoms: pods pending with `Insufficient GPUs` while autoscaler shows scale attempts or fails.
- Steps: check cluster-autoscaler logs, verify cloud quotas, inspect launch template user-data, re-trigger scale via `infra/ops/scale.sh` (approver required).

Terraform emergency rollback

1. If apply causes disruption, run `terraform destroy` only against introduced resources where safe, or revert to previous state using state snapshot.
2. Notify stakeholders, open incident ticket, coordinate with security and SRE.

Oncall escalation matrix

- 0-10m: primary oncall handles alerts and mitigation.
- 10-30m: notify oncall lead and engineering manager.
- 30-60m: engage infra-incident-response and PagerDuty second tier; consider war room.

Operational tooling & commands

- Check GPU nodes: `kubectl get nodes -l accelerator=nvidia -o wide`
- Driver logs: `journalctl -u nvidia-driver -o short-iso`
- Prometheus query (GPU util): `sum(rate(nvidia_gpu_utilization[5m])) by (region)`
- Manual scale script: `infra/ops/scale.sh --pool prod-gpu-h100 --delta +4`

Docs & onboarding

- Keep runbooks concise; detailed design belongs in architecture docs under /confluence/eng-infra/architecture-and-standards.
- New engineers: follow infra onboarding checklist and complete ephemeral cluster lab.

Appendix: quick Terraform staging apply

1. Authenticate: `gcloud auth login --account=infra-deployer@redwood.com` or `aws sso login --profile infra-deploy`
2. Workspace: `terraform workspace new staging || terraform workspace select staging`
3. Plan: `terraform plan -var-file=staging.tfvars -out=tfplan`
4. Apply (after approvals): `terraform apply tfplan`

Notes & roadmap

- Short-term: standardize module outputs for cost attribution and automated tagging.
- Medium-term: add simulated autoscaler load tests in CI before large reserved purchases.
- Long-term: evaluate multi-cloud fallback patterns for critical customers to reduce single-region risk.
